chapters.name: Chapter 1: Seeing your field in parts

lessons.title: Lesson 1: What precision agriculture is, on a small farm
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: List the differences within one of your fields that you could manage separately.
This lesson builds toward: Walking one of your own fields, you will list the differences within the field that precision agriculture could act on, naming at least three differences and how you saw each one.
Precision agriculture means managing the parts of a field differently, because they are different. One corner of a maize field may be sandy and dry, the low end waterlogged, and the middle rich because cattle were kept there. Treating the whole field the same wastes fertilizer and seed in some parts and starves others.
On big farms this is done with tractors that change their rate automatically. On a smallholding you can do the same thing by hand: more manure where the soil is poor, drainage in the wet patch, a different variety on the dry ridge, or no fertilizer where the crop never pays. The idea is the same: observe, measure, decide by zone, and check the result.
You already know a lot by eye. Walk the field and note where the crop is short, yellow or patchy, where water stands, where weeds like Striga appear, and where yields were good or bad. Ask the workers who weed and harvest: they see every corner. Satellite maps, GPS and soil tests, in the next lessons, help you confirm and measure what you see.
Step by step:
- Walk the whole field, edge and middle.
- Note where the crop is weak, where water stands, where weeds or pests are worse.
- Ask workers where yields are good or bad.
- Write each difference and how you saw it.
- Mark them on a rough sketch of the field.
Words to know:
- Precision agriculture: managing different parts of a field differently, based on observation and measurement.
- Variability: how much soil, water or crop growth changes from one part of a field to another.
- Management zone: a part of a field that is managed as one unit because it behaves in a similar way.
Try it now: Walk one of your fields. Draw a rough sketch and mark at least three differences (for example a weak patch, a wet patch, a weedy patch). Next to each, write how you saw it: by eye, from yields, or from workers.
You can now see a field as parts that differ, and list the differences you could manage separately.

check.q: What is the main idea of precision agriculture?
options: Managing different parts of a field differently
check.why: It gives each part of the field what it needs.

check.q: Who can tell you quickly where yields are poor in a field?
options: The workers who weed and harvest it
check.why: Workers see every corner of the field through the season.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Free satellite maps and what NDVI shows
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Compare your field's NDVI on two dates in a free satellite viewer.
This lesson builds toward: Using a free satellite viewer such as the Copernicus Browser, you will find your field and compare its NDVI on two dates, and say one thing the map shows and one thing it cannot show.
The European Sentinel-2 satellites photograph the whole of Africa about every 5 days, with pixels of 10 metres (one pixel is a 10 m x 10 m square). The images are free and open. The Copernicus Browser lets you view them without paying; you can start without an account, and a free account gives more options. Digital Earth Africa also offers free satellite services, such as NDVI anomaly and cropland maps, built for Africa.
NDVI (Normalised Difference Vegetation Index) is a number from the colours plants reflect. Healthy, dense green leaves give high NDVI; bare soil, dry or sparse crop gives low NDVI. In the viewer, find your field, choose an NDVI view, and compare two dates, for example four and eight weeks after planting. A patch that stays low when the rest is high is worth walking.
What NDVI does NOT show: the cause. Low NDVI can be drought, waterlogging, nitrogen shortage, pests, disease, weeds or a late planting. It also cannot see under clouds, and in the rainy season you may wait weeks for a clear image. On fields smaller than about half a hectare, or long narrow plots, 10 m pixels are coarse and mix in the neighbour's crop or trees. Weeds can also look green and healthy. So NDVI tells you where to look, and your feet tell you why.
Step by step:
- Open the Copernicus Browser on a computer or phone browser.
- Search your area and zoom to your field.
- Choose an image with little cloud and an NDVI view.
- Compare two dates in the same season.
- Mark low patches on your sketch and walk them to find the cause.
Words to know:
- Sentinel-2: a pair of European satellites that take free images of the earth about every 5 days at 10 m detail.
- NDVI: a number from satellite colours that shows how green and dense the plants are.
- Pixel: one square of a satellite image; for Sentinel-2, 10 m x 10 m.
Official sources:
- Copernicus Data Space Ecosystem and Copernicus Browser (free and open Sentinel data)
- European Space Agency: Sentinel-2 (10 m resolution, 5-day revisit)
- Digital Earth Africa (free satellite services, including NDVI anomalies and cropland maps)
Try it now: Open the Copernicus Browser, find one of your fields (or a field near you), and look at NDVI on two clear dates this season. Mark any low patch on your sketch, then walk it and write what you think the cause is.
You can now read a free satellite NDVI map of your field and use it to decide where to look, not what the cause is.

check.q: A patch of your maize field has low NDVI. What does that tell you?
options: Plants there are less green or sparse, so walk it and find out why
check.why: NDVI shows where growth is weak, not the cause.

check.q: Why can a free Sentinel-2 map be hard to use on a 0.2 hectare plot?
options: The 10 m pixels are coarse and mix in neighbouring land
The images are only for Europe
NDVI does not work on maize
check.why: A 0.2 ha plot is only a couple of dozen pixels, many mixed with its edges.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Mapping a field with your phone's GPS
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Record a field boundary and its zones with a phone GPS app and read their areas.
This lesson builds toward: Using a phone GPS app, you will record a field boundary and the edges of its zones and read their areas, allowing for an error of about 5 metres.
A phone's GPS can map your field. Many free apps can record a walked boundary or let you drop points around the field and then show the area. You can also drop a pin on a map app and share its coordinates. Knowing the real size of a field and each zone matters: fertilizer, seed, labour and yield per acre or hectare all depend on it, and many farmers find their field is bigger or smaller than they thought.
GPS is not exact. Under open sky, smartphones are typically accurate to within about 5 metres, and worse near trees, buildings and in valleys. On a small plot that error matters: walk slowly, stand still a few seconds at each corner, keep the phone in open sky, and walk the boundary twice to compare. If the two areas differ a lot, walk it again.
Map the zones too. Walk the edge of the wet patch or the sandy ridge and save it as a separate shape, or drop pins at its corners. Name each shape with the field and zone ("F2 Zone A wet"), and save the file or a screenshot with the area. These shapes become the base of your zone map in Lesson 6.
Step by step:
- Open a GPS area or mapping app outdoors with open sky.
- Walk the field boundary slowly, pausing at each corner.
- Read and record the area; walk it again to check.
- Walk or pin the edges of each zone and save each one with a name.
- Save the file or a screenshot with the areas.
Words to know:
- GPS: Global Positioning System: satellites that let a phone find where it is on the earth.
- Boundary: the edge of a field.
- Hectare: an area of 100 m x 100 m, about 2.5 acres.
Official sources:
- GPS.gov: GPS accuracy (smartphones about 4.9 m under open sky)
Try it now: Use a phone GPS app to walk the boundary of one field twice and write both areas. Then map the edge of one zone you found in Lesson 1, name it, and write its area.
You can now map a field and its zones with phone GPS and record their areas, allowing for GPS error.

check.q: You walked a field boundary twice and got 0.9 acres and 1.4 acres. What do you do?
options: Walk it again slowly, pausing at corners, in open sky
check.why: A big difference means poor readings; walk again carefully.

check.q: Where is phone GPS usually least accurate?
check.why: Trees and buildings block and reflect satellite signals.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Measuring soil and planning by zone

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Soil test kits and sensors: how far to trust them
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Choose a soil test method for each zone and say how far to trust its results.
This lesson builds toward: Given the choice of a laboratory test, a test kit or a handheld sensor, you will choose a soil test method, take a sample from each zone and say how far to trust each result, trusting pH more than nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium readings from kits.
There are three main ways to test soil. A laboratory test (from a national research institute such as KALRO, a university or an accredited private lab) is the most accurate, takes days to weeks and costs more. A field test kit (colour strips or chemicals in tubes) gives quick results on the spot. A handheld electronic sensor or meter gives a reading in minutes and is often sold with an app.
Independent tests of portable kits, such as an evaluation by IFDC, found good agreement with laboratories for soil pH but inconsistent results for nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium. Research in Embu County, Kenya, found that some advanced handheld sensors can predict several soil properties well, but those instruments are costly and need calibration against lab samples. Be careful with cheap probes that claim to read NPK instantly: sellers' own accuracy figures are not independent proof.
A practical plan: send one good composite sample per zone to a lab every few years, and use a kit or meter for quick checks of pH between lab tests. Take each sample the same way (many small cores, mixed, from the same depth, avoiding paths and manure heaps). The free iSDAsoil maps estimate soil properties across Africa at 30 m and are useful to see the general picture, but they are estimates from models, not a test of your field.
Step by step:
- Decide: lab test, kit or sensor, for each question you have.
- Take a composite sample per zone: many cores, same depth, mixed.
- Send the samples to an accredited lab every few years.
- Use a kit or meter for quick pH checks in between.
- Write each result next to its zone, with its method.
Words to know:
- Composite sample: many small soil cores from one zone mixed into one sample.
- Calibration: checking and adjusting a sensor against a trusted lab result.
- pH: a measure of how acid or alkaline soil is.
Official sources:
- IFDC: Evaluation of portable soil testing kits, lessons learned
- Performance evaluation of proximal sensors for soil assessment in smallholder farms in Embu County, Kenya
- iSDAsoil: continent-scale soil property maps for Africa at 30 m (PLOS Biology, 2021)
- Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization (KALRO)
Try it now: For each zone on your sketch, write which test you will use (lab, kit or sensor) and why. Take, or plan, one composite sample per zone, and write how far you would trust a kit result for pH and for nitrogen.
You can now choose a soil test method for each zone and judge how far to trust its results.

check.q: For which result are portable soil kits most reliable, compared with a lab?
check.why: Independent tests found good pH agreement but inconsistent N, P and K.

check.q: A seller says his cheap probe reads NPK instantly with 95 percent accuracy. You should:
options: Ask for independent test results and compare a few readings with a lab
Use it instead of all lab tests
Believe it because it has an app
check.why: Sellers' own figures are not independent proof; compare with a lab.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Costs versus benefits, and when drones help
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Compare the cost of a precision tool or practice with its expected benefit.
This lesson builds toward: Given a precision tool or practice and your field's numbers, you will compare its cost with its expected benefit and decide whether to use it, using a simple partial budget in local currency.
A precision tool only makes sense if the benefit is bigger than the cost. Use a simple partial budget: what extra will I earn or save (more yield, less fertilizer or seed wasted), and what extra will it cost (the test, the sensor, the app, your time, the labour)? Example only: if zoning saves 2 bags of fertilizer on a weak zone that never paid (2 x GHS 400 = GHS 800 saved), and the lab test cost GHS 300, it pays.
On small farms, start with what is free or cheap: your eyes, records, phone GPS and free satellite maps. Spend on a lab test per zone next. Buy a handheld sensor only if you will use it often and can check it against a lab. Groups can share costs: a cooperative in Côte d'Ivoire or a farmer group in Nigeria can buy one meter or pay for lab tests together.
Drones give images of a few centimetres instead of 10 metres, fly below the clouds, and can fly the day you need. They help on high-value crops, larger fields, or for a group buying a service together. They cost far more, and flying them needs a licence from the civil aviation authority. If you think you need one, take the "Drones for Agricultural Monitoring" courses and "Agricultural Drones: Data Analytics and Precision Agriculture"; this course does not repeat them.
Step by step:
- Write what the tool or practice costs: money, time, labour.
- Write the extra income or saving you expect, with example numbers.
- Compare: benefit minus cost.
- Start with free tools; then a lab test per zone; then a sensor or drone service only if it pays.
- Consider sharing costs with a group.
Words to know:
- Partial budget: a simple sum of only the extra costs and extra benefits of one change.
- Drone service: a business that flies a drone over your field for a fee.
- Return: what you get back for what you spend.
Try it now: Pick one precision tool or practice for your farm (a lab test per zone, a soil meter, a drone service, or zoned fertilizer). Write a partial budget with example local-currency numbers: extra cost, extra benefit, and your decision.
You can now decide whether a precision tool is worth it for your farm with a simple partial budget.

check.q: On a small farm, which should you usually try first?
options: Your eyes, records, phone GPS and free satellite maps
check.why: Start with free tools and spend only where it pays.

check.q: A soil meter costs more than you would save in five seasons. What is a sensible choice?
options: Share the cost through a group, or use lab tests instead
check.why: If the benefit does not beat the cost alone, share it or choose a cheaper method.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Making a field zone map and a plan for each zone
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Divide a field into 2 to 4 zones and write a plan for each zone.
This lesson builds toward: Given evidence from at least two sources, you will divide a field into 2 to 4 management zones and write a plan for each zone, each plan affordable and checkable next season. Given a precision tool or practice and your field's numbers, you will compare its cost with its expected benefit and decide whether to use it, using a simple partial budget in local currency.
Now put the evidence together. Lay your GPS shapes over your sketch. For each part of the field, list what you know: NDVI on two dates, soil test or kit results, past yields, what you and the workers see. A zone needs at least two kinds of evidence that agree, for example low NDVI and a low pH result, or a wet patch seen every season and poor yields recorded.
Keep it simple: 2 to 4 zones are enough on a smallholding. Name them by what they are: "Zone A good soil", "Zone B acid and weak", "Zone C waterlogged". Write each zone's area from your GPS map.
Then write a plan for each zone: what you will do differently (more compost and lime where pH is low as the lab advises; drains or a rice or vegetable crop in the wet zone; a lower fertilizer rate where the crop never pays), what it will cost as an example in your currency, and how you will check it: record yield by zone at harvest and compare NDVI next season. Use only registered fertilizers and pesticides, as the label says. A precision plan is only right if next season's records show it worked.
Step by step:
- Put GPS shapes, NDVI notes, soil results and yields on one map.
- Draw 2 to 4 zones where two kinds of evidence agree.
- Name each zone and write its area.
- Write a plan, cost and check for each zone.
- Record yield by zone at harvest and compare next season.
Words to know:
- Zone map: a map of a field divided into management zones.
- Evidence: facts you can point to, such as a test result, an NDVI image or a yield record.
- Lime: a soil treatment that makes acid soil less acid.
Try it now: Final task: make the zone map of your field with 2 to 4 zones, each labelled with its area and at least two kinds of evidence. Write a plan for each zone: the change, the example cost in your currency, and how you will check next season whether it worked.
You can now make a field zone map from several kinds of evidence and write a checkable plan for each zone.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Field and zones mapped No boundary, or areas guessed. Boundary walked with GPS and each zone has a named shape and area. Boundary walked twice and the areas agree closely. Satellite evidence used carefully No satellite view, or NDVI treated as the cause. NDVI compared on two dates and low patches walked to find the cause. Notes what the map could not show (clouds, small plots, weeds) for this field. Soil evidence No soil information, or kit NPK readings treated as exact. A test method chosen for each zone with how far it can be trusted. At least one lab result per zone, or kit readings compared with a lab. Zones and plans Zones drawn from one source, or no plan per zone. 2 to 4 zones, each with two kinds of evidence and a plan, cost and check. Each plan names the record that will show whether it worked next season. Worth the cost Tools chosen without counting cost. A partial budget with example local-currency numbers supports the plan. Considers sharing costs with a group, or a cheaper method that gives the same answer. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Which is enough evidence to draw a zone?
options: Low NDVI on one cloudy date
Low NDVI on two dates and a low pH soil result
check.why: Two kinds of evidence that agree make a zone reliable.

check.q: How will you know a zone plan worked?
options: Record yield by zone at harvest and compare next season
check.why: Only records by zone show whether the change paid.
